abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Both anti-CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy and CD20xCD3 bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) are recommended as preferred regimens of third-line and subsequent treatment for follicular lymphoma (FL). We aimed to compare the efficacy and safety of CAR-T and BsAbs in third- or later-line treatments for relapsed or refractory (R/R) FL. We reviewed trials from PubMed, Embase and Cochrane Library databases up to January 31, 2025. Primary endpoint was overall response rate (ORR). Secondary endpoints included complete response rate (CRR), 12-month progression-free survival (PFS), and grade ≥ 3 adverse events of cytokine release syndrome (CRS), neurotoxicity, and infection. Eight studies comprising 725 grade 1-3a FL patients with R/R disease after ≥ 2 lines of systemic therapy were included in the meta-analysis. The pooled ORR was 0.93 (95% CI, 0.84–0.97) for CAR-T and 0.81 (95% CI, 0.77–0.85) for BsAbs (P = 0.02). For safety profiles, no significant difference was observed between the two groups in terms of grade ≥ 3 CRS, neurotoxicity, and infections. Anti-CD19 CAR-T cell therapy exhibited higher ORR compared to CD20xCD3 BsAbs as third- or later-line treatment for R/R FL with comparable toxicities.

sec.p: Keywords: Anti-CD19 CAR-T, CD20xCD3 bispecific antibody, Relapsed or refractory, Follicular lymphoma

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Follicular lymphoma (FL) is the most common subtype of indolent non-Hodgkin lymphoma [1]. While frontline anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody-based chemoimmunotherapy results in superior response and survival, disease with advanced stage is still incurable, most of which will eventually relapse after initial remission or become refractory to treatment, and with each recurrence or drug resistance, the response rate, duration of remission and survival will gradually worsen [2–4]. 20–25% of patients may relapse or progress within 24 months after initial treatment with chemoimmunotherapy (POD 24), whose prognosis is poor [5]. There are no standardized treatment strategies for relapsed or refractory (R/R) FL patients. Both European Medicines Agency (EMA) and Food and Drug Administration (FDA) have approved rituximab, obinutuzumab in combination with bendamustine followed by obinutuzumab monotherapy, lenalidomide in combination with rituximab, mosunetuzumab, axicabtagene ciloleucel, lisocabtagene maraleucel, tisagenlecleucel, epcoritamab for adult patients with R/R FL. In addition, EMA has approved idelalisib, duvelisib, and odronextamab for R/R FL, whereas idelalisib and duvelisib were withdrawn and odronextamab is under evaluation by FDA. Tazemetostat, zanubrutinib with obinutuzumab, and tafasitamab-cxix with lenalidomide and rituximab were approved by FDA, not EMA approved. Treatment choices beyond second-line therapies have been limited, with challenges including cumulative toxicity, diminishing efficacy, and antigen escape mechanisms. T-cell engager therapy including CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapy and CD20xCD3 bispecific antibodies (BsAbs) have emerged as revolutionary immunotherapies for R/R FL, offering distinct mechanisms of action and clinical profiles that warrant comparative evaluation.

Two CD19-directed CAR-T cell products, tisagenlecleucel and lisocabtagene maraleucel, were approved for R/R FL after two or more lines of systemic therapy by both EMA and FDA based on the results of ELARA and TRANSCEND FL trials [6, 7]. Another CAR-T therapy, axicabtagene ciloleucel, was approved after three or more prior lines of treatment by EMA and after two or more lines of therapy by FDA based on ZUMA-5 [8]. Three CD20xCD3 T-cell engaging bispecific antibodies which result in high response rate and durable remission with manageable safety profiles, including mosunetuzumab, epcoritamab, and odronextamab have been approved for treatment of adult patients with R/R FL who have received at least two prior systemic therapies by EMA [9–11]. Mosunetuzumab and epcoritamab were approved for the same indication by FDA, whereas odronextamab has not yet been approved by FDA. There have been no randomized controlled trials comparing the effectiveness and safety of these two T-cell engager therapies. A meta-analysis comparing CAR-T and BsAbs in R/R diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) revealed superior complete response for CAR-T but higher incidence of grade ≥ 3 cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity [12]. While FL-specific data are sparse, necessitating relevant evidence to guide clinical practice. By pooling existing studies on CD19 CAR-T and CD20xCD3 BsAbs in R/R FL, we perform this meta-analysis aimed to evaluate their efficacy and safety profiles and inform clinical decision-making in third- or later-line treatments for R/R FL.

sec.title: Search strategy
sec.p: The systematic literature review and meta-analysis were performed following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses methodology. This study has been registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) web registry. Literature retrieval was conducted on PubMed, Embase, and the Cochrane Library, limiting in English with the time of entries up to January 31, 2025. A combination of Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free-text terms was employed. Keywords included: “lymphoma, non hodgkin”, “lymphoma, b cell”, “lymphoma, follicular”, “relapse”, “refractory”, “recurrence”, “previously treated”, “third-line”, “immunotherapy, adoptive”, “chimeric antigen receptor”, “CAR-T”, “CART-19”, “antibodies, bispecific”, and related derivative terms. Additionally, manual searching the references of included studies were performed to supplement potentially omitted relevant trials. All searches were independently executed by two investigators and subsequently verified by a third investigator.

sec.title: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
sec.p: This meta-analysis included studies evaluating the efficacy and safety of CD19 CAR-T cell therapy or CD20xCD3 bispecific antibodies as third- or later-line treatment in adult patients with relapsed/refractory follicular lymphoma, including prospective randomized controlled clinical trials or single-arm studies. Phase I trials which established the recommended phase II dose and evaluated efficacy were also incorporated. Exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) duplicate publications; (2) non-original studies such as reviews, case reports, or commentaries; (3) studies lacking critical data necessary for quantitative synthesis. For multiple publications of the same study, only the publication featuring the longest follow-up or most complete data was retained.

sec.title: Data extraction and quality assessment
sec.p: Two investigators independently screened the literature. Titles and abstracts were reviewed first for preliminary screening to exclude distinctly irrelevant studies. Full texts were then assessed for final inclusion. The following data were independently extracted by both researchers: (1) basic information including first author, publication year, study region, study design, demographic and clinical characteristics of the study population; (2) interventions encompassing type of CAR-T cell therapy or bispecific antibody, dosage, administration route, and treatment cycle; (3) outcomes including overall response rate, complete response rate, partial response rate, duration of response, progression-free survival, overall survival, and incidence of grade ≥ 3 adverse events, including cytokine release syndrome, neurologic events, and infection; (4) follow-up period. Discrepancies were discussed by the two investigators or arbitrated by a third investigator.

sec.title: Risk of bias assessment
sec.p: The Cochrane tool for bias risk assessment was used to evaluate the quality of randomized controlled trials (RCTs), focusing on six domains of bias including generation of randomized sequence, concealment of allocation, blinding of investigators and participants, blinding of outcome assessment, incomplete data of outcome, selective reporting, and other biases. For non-randomized controlled trials and single-arm studies, the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) was applied to assess quality, with scores assigned across three characteristics: selection of study participants (maximum 4 points), comparability (maximum 2 points), and outcome assessment (maximum 3 points). A total score of ≥ 7 out of 9 indicated high-quality studies. Quality assessments were independently conducted by two investigators, and discrepancies were discussed or arbitrated by a third investigator.

sec.title: Data synthesis and analysis
sec.p: The primary endpoint was overall response rate (ORR), and secondary endpoints included complete response rate (CRR), 12-month progression-free survival (PFS), and grade ≥ 3 adverse events of cytokine release syndrome (CRS), neurologic events, and infection. This study was a single-arm meta-analysis of proportions for the primary and secondary outcomes. Study-specific proportions were logit-transformed to stabilize variances. The pooled proportions were estimated using random-effects models, with weights assigned by the inverse-variance method. Between-study variance τ² was calculated via restricted maximum likelihood (REML). Heterogeneity was quantified using the I² and τ² statistics. Subgroup analyses were performed to compare the two treatment modalities using the Q test. The Hartung–Knapp adjustments were applied to derive 95% confidence intervals. A two-sided P-value ≤ 0.05 was considered significant. Statistical analyses were conducted using R studio software version 4.4.2.

sec.title: Search of literature and characteristics of studies
sec.p: According to the search strategy, 3061 records were screened and 191 were assessed for eligibility (Fig. 1). Finally, a total of eight studies comprising 725 patients were included, consisting of three studies on CAR-T cell therapy and five studies on bispecific antibodies. The baseline characteristics of included studies are summarized in Table 1. All studies were single-arm, multicenter clinical trials which enrolled adult patients with relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma who had received two or more previous lines of therapy, six of which were phase Ⅱ and two were phase Ⅰ. The three studies on CAR-T cell therapy investigated lisocabtagene maraleucel, tisagenlecleucel, and axicabtagene ciloleucel, respectively, otherwise the five trials on bispecific antibody studied epcoritamab (one), mosunetuzumab (two), and odronextamab (two), respectively.

sec.title: Quality assessment of included studies
sec.p: Since all included studies were single-arm, the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS) was applied for quality assessment, focusing on selection of study participants, comparability, and outcome evaluation. Most studies demonstrated clear inclusion and exclusion criteria, provided detailed reports on follow-up procedures and methods of outcome assessment, which were considered with high quality. Detailed scoring results are presented in Table 2.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: The overall pooled proportion of ORR was 0.87 (95% CI, 0.80–0.91). A statistically significant difference was observed between the two groups (P = 0.02), with an ORR of 0.93 (95% CI, 0.84–0.97) for CAR-T cell therapy and 0.81 (95% CI, 0.77–0.85) for bispecific antibody (Fig. 2). The overall pooled proportion of CRR was 0.74 (95% CI, 0.64–0.82). CAR-T showed a non-significantly higher CRR (0.83, 95% CI, 0.62–0.94) compared to bispecific antibody (0.67, 95% CI, 0.60–0.73) (P = 0.13) (Fig. 3). The overall pooled proportion of 12-month PFS was 0.71 (95% CI, 0.62–0.79). CAR-T demonstrated superior 12-month PFS (0.77, 95% 0.67–0.84) compared to bispecific antibody (0.63, 95% CI 0.54–0.70) (P = 0.03) (Fig. 4).

sec.title: Adverse events
sec.p: The pooled analysis revealed an incidence of grade ≥ 3 CRS at 0.02 (95% CI, 0.00-0.09) in the CAR-T group and 0.03 (95% CI, 0.02–0.06) in the bispecific group with no difference existing (P = 0.60) (Fig. 5). The CAR-T group reported a non-significantly elevated rate of grade ≥ 3 neurologic toxicity (0.05, 95% CI, 0.01–0.18) versus the bispecific antibody group (0.03, 95% CI 0.01–0.12) (Fig. 6), whereas the bispecific antibody group presented a non-significantly higher incidence of grade ≥ 3 infections (0.18, 95% CI, 0.04–0.52) in contrast to CAR-T (0.08, 95% CI, 0.03–0.17) (Fig. 7).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This meta-analysis demonstrated CAR-T cell therapy exhibited significantly higher overall response, 12-month PFS, and non-significantly elevated complete response compared to bispecific antibody as third- or later-line therapy in patients with R/R follicular lymphoma, which aligned with previous research. An unanchored matching-adjusted indirect comparison of efficacy and safety of lisocabtagene maraleucel and mosunetuzumab for the treatment of third-line or later relapsed or refractory FL revealed that CAR-T was associated with higher ORR, CRR, and improved duration of response and PFS compared with bispecific antibody [16]. A meta-analysis which evaluated the efficacy and safety of CAR-T cell therapy and bispecific antibodies for R/R DLBCL also showed a higher CRR and 1-year PFS of CAR-T compared to bispecific antibodies [12].

The superior efficacy of CAR-T cell therapy could be attributed to the potent and persistent anti-tumor activity of CAR-T cells which exhibited enhanced tumor-killing capacity and proliferative potential through engineering in vitro, and demonstrated sustained existence in vivo to exert anti-tumor activity for long-term disease control. In addition, CAR-T cells employed multiple effector mechanisms, including direct cell-killing, induction apoptosis of tumor cells, and activation of endogenous antitumor immunity [17, 18]. In contrast, while bispecific antibodies could simultaneously engage tumor cells and T cells to mediate synergistic cell-killing, they exhibited limitations in pharmacokinetic persistence and clonal expansion capacity [19].

Prominent toxicities associated with the two therapeutic modalities involved CRS, neurological events, and infection, both of which demonstrated manageable toxicity profiles. This study indicated comparable incidence of severe CRS, which remained the most prevalent acute adverse event of CAR-T intervention, primarily mediated by massive cytokines release including interleukin-6 (IL-6), interferon-γ (IFN-γ), tumor necrosis factor (TNF), IL-2, IL-2–receptor-α, IL-8, and IL-10 after CAR-T cells infusion [20]. While treatment with bispecific antibodies also resulted in CRS due to T-cell activation and degranulation, and the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-2, IL-6, IFN-γ, and TNF-α [21]. Administration of tocilizumab, an IL-6 receptor antagonist, has been shown to effectively treat CRS-related toxicities [20].

Neurotoxicity represented a distinct adverse event of particular concern with CAR-T cell therapy, although the pathogenesis of which remained incompletely understood. Potential mechanisms could involve disruption and increased permeability of blood-brain barrier, which allowed for infiltration of cytokines and immune cells (including CAR-T cells) into central nervous system [22]. Our investigation revealed a slightly lower incidence of grade ≥ 3 neurologic events in the bispecific antibody group versus the CAR-T group. Previous studies have reported CD20xCD3 BsAbs presented less frequent and lower grade of neurologic events compared to CD19-directed CAR-T and CD19xCD3 BsAbs, with a median rate ranging from 0% to 12% in the CD20xCD3 BsAbs [23]. Early recognition and prompt intervention were of paramount importance for neurotoxicity.

Infection was common in cellular immunotherapy, primarily attributable to treatment-related immunosuppression and cytokine storm-induced tissue damage. Our results identified a mildly increased rate at 0.18 for infections of grade ≥ 3 in the BsAbs group compared with CAR-T. The ELM-2 study investigating odronextamab reported the highest incidence of grade ≥ 3 infections at 42.2% in contrast to studies of mosunetuzumab indicating less frequent severe infections, possibly due to the difference in the treatment duration, fixed duration for mosunetuzumab (a maximum of 17 21-day cycles), until progression or unacceptable toxicity for odronextamab [11, 13, 14]. Similarly, a previous meta-analysis estimating infection risks associated with CD20-directed BsAb in patients with B-cell lymphoma revealed 20% of patients experienced a grade ≥ 3 infection, with the highest incidence reported in trials of odronextamab [24]. The notable infection occurring in BsAbs treatment might correlated to multiple factors. Patients with relapsed or refractory disease have received multiple lines of therapy, which increased their risk of infection. Additionally, continuous T-cell stimulation by repeated dosing of BsAbs could induce T-cell exhaustion, weakening cell-mediated immunity [25]. Moreover, impaired B-cell function by anti-CD20 BsAbs caused hypogammaglobulinemia, weakening humoral immunity.

A limitation of this meta-analysis is that some included studies have relatively short duration of follow-up, which necessitates further validation of long-term efficacy and safety profiles. Other limitations include pooling unadjusted data from heterogeneous sources, and the relatively limited number of studies due to lack of clinical trials, and these warrant further investigation before definitive conclusions about efficacy should be made.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: This study indicated anti-CD19 CAR-T cell therapy exhibited higher ORR compared to CD20xCD3 bispecific antibodies as third- or later-line treatment for relapsed or refractory follicular lymphoma, with comparable toxicities between the two groups. It should be noted the limits of an indirect comparison between treatments in the absence of direct randomized comparison. Further prospective, randomized controlled trials are warranted.

sec.title: Registration
sec.p: This study was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO) web registry. The registration number for this review is CRD420251005804.
